title: Peaceful protest and assembly
summary: The First Amendment protects speech and peaceful assembly, but time, place, and manner rules and other applicable laws can affect particular events.
steps: Review local permit rules and official notices before an event.
Identify public spaces and lawful assembly requirements without assuming all restrictions are valid.
If approached by officials, remain calm, avoid physical interference, and ask for legal assistance when appropriate.
Record the time, location, agency, and relevant orders after an incident when safe.
cautions: Emergency declarations do not automatically suspend constitutional rights.
Restrictions and enforcement can change; consult current local law and qualified counsel.

sources.title: ACLU — Know Your Rights: Protesters' Rights

title: Documenting public encounters
summary: Recording officials performing public duties in public places may receive constitutional protection, subject to applicable limits and circumstances.
steps: Stay at a safe distance and do not interfere with official duties.
Preserve original files, timestamps, and context; avoid altering the original evidence.
Document what happened accurately, including facts that do not support your initial interpretation.
Consider the privacy of bystanders and vulnerable people before sharing footage.
cautions: Audio recording and private-property rules vary by state and situation.
A general right to record does not guarantee access to restricted areas.

title: Device and account security
summary: Basic security practices can reduce accidental exposure of personal information and improve account resilience.
steps: Keep operating systems and apps updated.
Use a strong device passcode and multifactor authentication for important accounts.
Review app permissions, location sharing, photo metadata, and cloud backup settings.
Prepare emergency contact information and consider how you would recover an account or lost device.
cautions: Encryption does not conceal all communications metadata.
No device setting guarantees anonymity or protection from lawful legal process.

title: Private and reliable communications
summary: Understand the differences between encrypted content, identifying metadata, public posts, and ordinary phone or SMS communications.
steps: Choose reputable end-to-end encrypted messaging for sensitive lawful discussions.
Verify contacts and avoid forwarding unconfirmed claims.
Have an offline communication and meeting plan if cellular service is unavailable.
Avoid publicly posting identifying details of bystanders without consent.
cautions: End-to-end encryption does not eliminate all metadata.
Connectivity and emergency communications can fail during large gatherings.

title: Preserving evidence responsibly
summary: Accurate, contextual documentation is essential for oversight, public records work, and potential legal proceedings.
steps: Preserve unedited originals and record when and how evidence was obtained.
Maintain a clear timeline of events and distinguish firsthand observations from secondhand reports.
Back up files securely and limit access to sensitive personal information.
Consult counsel or a qualified organization before publishing identifying evidence.
cautions: Do not publish private addresses, sensitive personal data, or unverified accusations.
CIVIC WATCH does not currently accept evidence uploads.

title: Emergency powers and legal changes
summary: Emergency declarations, curfews, and deployments can alter applicable rules, but their scope depends on the legal authority and facts.
steps: Locate the actual emergency order, effective dates, and jurisdiction.
Compare official announcements with the text of the order.
Consult local civil liberties groups or legal counsel about challenges and exceptions.
Keep dated copies of orders and related public statements for accountability research.
cautions: Martial law and emergency declarations are not interchangeable terms.
Do not assume any specific order is valid or invalid without legal analysis.
